problem.after:
None of `/plan-docs`'s edit rules fires when documentation departs from its docspec's reader or coverage. An owner who changes whom a kind of documentation is for, or what it covers, never sees the documentation change.

A docspec is the owner's order for one kind of documentation: where it lives, its reader (`## Reader`), what it covers (`## Covers`), and its shape. `/plan-docs` plans a documentation sprint for each docspec whose text or references changed since its stamp, the commit its documentation was last checked at. The writer edits a file only where one of six rules fires: a false claim, a missing public element, a shown internal element, a sprint that changed what a user can do, a departure from the shape or layout, or a claim no one can settle. Every other sentence stays as written. [decision:documentation-edits-only-where-a-rule-fires](.ok-planner/design/decisions/documentation-edits-only-where-a-rule-fires.md) fixes those six rules, and [plan-docs core.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-docs/core.md#L7-L25) carries them.

In a test run, an agent changed a stamped docspec's reader and coverage. `/plan-docs` reached the docspec, but no rule fired on the existing file. The plan held no item, and the stamp moved past the change. A docspec first declared over existing documentation has the same gap.

[story:declare-project-documentation](.ok-planner/design/stories/declare-project-documentation.md) asks that "whoever writes that documentation writes what I asked for", including "whom it is for, and what it describes". A decision records how the project delivers a story, so the decision is the text to change. An owner could narrow the story instead, but no ruling has.

The ruling decides the edit rule that makes documentation follow its docspec's reader and coverage.

problem.after:
`/converge` starts the product under one fixed run name, `drive`, and after a failed start it stops whatever run holds that name. When a second run's start fails because a first run holds the name, the second run takes down the first run's live product.

A `/converge` drive tests the project's stories against the running product, its stack. The reference stack tool, `.ok-planner/bin/stack`, starts each stack as a run under a name. The drive's start line is `stack up --name drive`, and its stop line is `stack down --name drive`. `stack up` refuses where a live run already holds the name. After a failed start, drive step 2 runs the stop line to take down "what the failed start left". The stack helpers document says no run then holds the name. That holds only where the failed start opened the run. A refused start opened nothing.

In a scratch-project test, a first run started and served. A second run's start was refused because the first held the name. The second run's stop line then printed `took down: run-cfc94a3e1f1b (WEB_PORT=44856; 1 container(s), ...)`, and the first run's server was gone.

The site is [converge/SKILL.md:In drive mode step 2](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/converge/SKILL.md#L79), with the stop line in [ADMINISTRATION.md:Stack declaration](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/admin/ADMINISTRATION.md#L225) and [stack-helpers.md](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/stack-helpers.md#L438-L444). Accept-list entry A2 covers it: cleanup reaches something it did not create. The hook that lints each agent edit reads only a tool call's `file_path` input, so an edit made through Bash or the notebook editor lands unchecked. A Read of an untracked file that holds a comment, though, blocks the agent.

The lint checks a file for residue, such as prose comments. True-up, the step that installs the suite into a project, wires the hook to run after every tool call. The hook [reads only the input's `file_path`](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/hooks/post-edit.js#L41-L42) and passes when the input has none. A Bash call names no file, and NotebookEdit names its file in `notebook_path`. The lint also has [no grammar for `.ipynb` files](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/plumbline#L64-L91). Read carries `file_path` too, so the hook lints each file Read opens. Claude Code's auto mode tells agents they may make small edits through Bash.

[story:edit-time-lint-enforcement](.ok-planner/design/stories/edit-time-lint-enforcement.md) promises "every agent edit checked against the lint checks my project turned on as it lands". [decision:edit-hook-blocks-in-turn](.ok-planner/design/decisions/edit-hook-blocks-in-turn.md) scopes the hook to the edited file's changed lines, and does not say which tools count as edits. The [cheatsheet](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/docs/plumbline-cheatsheet.md#L161) says the hook "does nothing for a Bash call". The review loop lints changed files later.

A driver fed the wired hook Claude Code tool payloads. The hook checked Edit, Write, and MultiEdit. A Bash call that wrote a prose comment passed, and so did a NotebookEdit whose cell held one. A Read of an untracked file that holds a comment blocked.

The ruling decides whether the edit-time check covers edits made through Bash and notebooks.

The corpus is the project's design documents. `/discover-design` audits the code against it and hands `/plan-sprint` questions only the owner can answer, each with two drafted answers, as [decision:corpus-audit-hands-a-discovery-to-planning](.ok-planner/design/decisions/corpus-audit-hands-a-discovery-to-planning.md) requires. "The corpus is stale" carries a delta, a drafted change to one corpus file. "The code is wrong" carries a work item, a code change.

Where no document records the code's behavior, the audit proposes one. The [merge step](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/discover-design/core.md#L406-L411) drafts it, as the code has it, only as the stale answer. The wrong answer gets the work item and the sentence the document records once the code matches. The [audit tool](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/discover#L583) refuses any other draft of it. Under the wrong answer, the [planning walk](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/plan-sprint/SKILL.md#L91) carries the work item alone.

The corpus misses a change [story:bootstrap-design-corpus](.ok-planner/design/stories/bootstrap-design-corpus.md) promises. The next audit proposes the document again.

The ruling decides whether, and how, the code-is-wrong answer on a proposed document also adds it to the corpus.

recommendation.text:
Draft the proposed document under both answers. The audit writes a second body for each question on a proposed document: the document as the text at issue has it once the code matches. Planning carries that body under the code-is-wrong answer, as it carries the stale answer's body under the other.

Rationale: The corpus audit's decision gives every question both answers, and the audit's review fixes each draft before the owner sees it. So the owner spends attention on the choice, not on writing prose. Option A keeps both answers drafted and reviewed. Option B writes a body in the planning dialogue that no review read. Option C leaves the story's "corpus changes it needs" unmade, and the next audit asks again. The flip case: if questions on proposed documents prove rare, and the wrong answer's sentence nearly always carries the whole document, B costs less than a second body the audit must check.

problem.after:
The review tool reads a code block inside a sprint's change body in two different ways, and the sprint form gives no rule for fencing such a body. So sprint certification fails a sprint whose change landed exactly as approved, and can count a change the sprint never wrote.

A sprint carries each change to the design corpus as a corpus delta: a heading such as `### New decision: <slug>`, then the artifact's whole new text, its body, inside a `` ```markdown `` fence. Sprint certification, `/converge sprint`, runs the review tool to compare each landed file with its body. [decision:final-form-deltas](.ok-planner/design/decisions/final-form-deltas.md) makes that comparison the test, and [story:certify-completion](.ok-planner/design/stories/certify-completion.md) promises that "done" means the same thing for every sprint. The [delta form](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/skills/_shared/artifact-definitions.md#L277-L285) says nothing about a body that holds a code block.

To find delta headings, [review:fence_depths](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1565-L1574) lets an info-string line such as `` ```sh `` open a nested fence and a bare backtick line close the innermost one. [review:inline_body](plugins/ok/families/ok-planner/scripts/review#L1607-L1614) cuts each body at the first later line equal to its opening fence. CommonMark, the reading Markdown renderers use, differs from both: inside an open fence an info-string line is text, and the first bare closer at least as long ends the outer fence.

A three-backtick body holding a bare code block, landed byte for byte, fails as "differs from the delta's body". Two fixes were sent back. Ending the body at its last closer dropped the next delta from the count. Reading by depth still let a bare inner block close the outer fence, so a heading-like line inside it added a phantom delta or dropped a real one. Four-backtick fences read correctly.

The ruling decides how a delta body may hold a code block, and what the tool does with a body that breaks that rule.
